questions.question: What is weathering?
choices: The breaking down of rocks into smaller pieces
The transport of loose material to another place
The formation of new rock from melted material
The piling up of sediments in layers
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks down through physical or chemical processes.

questions.question: What makes weathering mechanical?
choices: Rocks combine with oxygen
Compounds react chemically with water
Carbonic acid reacts with minerals
Rocks are broken down by physical means
questions.explanation: Mechanical weathering breaks rock physically.

questions.question: Which group lists causes of mechanical weathering?
choices: Rust, carbonic acid, and acid rain
Sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide
Temperature, ice, water, and living things
Hydrolysis, carbonation, and oxidation
questions.explanation: The lesson lists temperature, ice, water, and living things as physical weathering agents.

questions.question: What is ice wedging?
choices: The downhill flow of mud after rain
Rock damage caused by repeated freezing and thawing
Rock breakdown by carbonic acid
Sediment sorting by melting glaciers
questions.explanation: Cycles of freezing and thawing damage rock through expansion.

questions.question: Why does freezing water help break a rock apart?
choices: It dissolves the rock through carbonation
It expands and pushes against the rock
It reacts with oxygen to form rust
It turns the entire rock into soil
questions.explanation: Ice wedging damages rock through the expansion of freezing water.

questions.question: How can temperature extremes cause rock material to separate?
choices: Materials expand at different rates
All minerals melt at the same temperature
Temperature changes always produce carbonic acid
Cold conditions turn rock into rust
questions.explanation: Different rates of expansion can cause materials in rock to separate.

questions.question: What can the mechanical action of tides cause along a rocky coast?
choices: Oxidation of every rock layer
The formation of glacial till
The downhill movement called soil creep
Uneven weathering
questions.explanation: The lesson describes tides as a cause of uneven mechanical weathering.

questions.question: Tree roots grow between stones and push them apart. What kind of weathering is this?
choices: Chemical weathering by carbonation
Chemical weathering by hydrolysis
Mechanical weathering by living things
Chemical weathering by oxidation
questions.explanation: Roots can physically damage and break down stone, as shown in the temple photographs.

questions.question: What is chemical weathering?
choices: The physical splitting of rocks by roots
The freezing of water in cracks
The breakdown of rocks by chemical processes
The transport of rocks without changing them
questions.explanation: Chemical weathering breaks down rock through chemical processes.

questions.question: Which example illustrates chemical weathering in the lesson?
choices: Tides physically wearing a coastal cliff
The green surface of the copper Statue of Liberty
Roots pushing apart temple stones
Ice expanding inside a rock crack
questions.explanation: The Statue of Liberty's copper surface is used as an example of chemical weathering.

questions.question: What is hydrolysis?
choices: The breakdown of a compound by a chemical reaction with water
The chemical combination of a substance with oxygen
The transport of sediment by moving water
The physical splitting of rock by freezing water
questions.explanation: Hydrolysis breaks down a compound through a chemical reaction with water.

questions.question: Which atmospheric gases are listed as reacting with water to form acid rain?
choices: Oxygen, helium, and hydrogen
Nitrogen, argon, and helium
Hydrogen, methane, and neon
Sulfur dioxides, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The lesson lists sulfur dioxides, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide reacting with atmospheric water and precipitating.

questions.question: What effect does acid rain have on chemical weathering?
choices: It stops it completely
It changes it into ice wedging
It prevents water from reacting with rock
It speeds it up
questions.explanation: Acid rain speeds up chemical weathering.

questions.question: Which human activity can accelerate acid rain?
choices: Moving rocks into the shade
Building a wind barrier
Burning fossil fuels
Planting trees on a hillside
questions.explanation: The lesson says acid rain can occur naturally and can be accelerated by burning fossil fuels.

questions.question: What is carbonation?
choices: The breaking of rock by temperature changes
The reaction of carbonic acid with other substances
The reaction of a substance with oxygen
The sorting of sediment by a glacier
questions.explanation: Carbonation is the process in which carbonic acid reacts with other substances.

questions.question: What is oxidation?
choices: A chemical change in which a substance combines with oxygen
A physical change caused by ice expansion
The removal of sediment by wind
The reaction of carbonic acid with other substances
questions.explanation: Oxidation occurs when a substance combines with oxygen.

questions.question: Which substance is an example of oxidation in the lesson?
choices: Iron oxide, or rust
Glacial till
Regolith
A mound of windblown sand
questions.explanation: Rust is iron oxide and is the lesson's example of oxidation.

questions.question: Water splits one rock by freezing and breaks down another through a chemical reaction. Which processes are involved, in that order?
choices: Hydrolysis and ice wedging
Carbonation and oxidation
Oxidation and carbonation
Ice wedging and hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Freezing and expansion cause ice wedging; a compound reacting chemically with water undergoes hydrolysis.

questions.question: Which rock group is generally most easily weathered, especially mechanically?
choices: Metamorphic rocks
All rock groups equally
Sedimentary rocks
Igneous rocks
questions.explanation: The lesson identifies sedimentary rocks as generally the most easily weathered, especially mechanically.

questions.question: Which rock does the lesson identify as easily weathered chemically?
choices: Basalt
Limestone
Granite
Quartzite
questions.explanation: Limestone is listed as easily weathered chemically.

questions.question: How does rock size affect weathering in the lesson?
choices: Small rocks cannot undergo mechanical weathering
Small rocks weather more quickly than large rocks
Large rocks always weather faster than small rocks
Rock size prevents all chemical weathering
questions.explanation: Under amount of exposure, the lesson states that small rocks weather more quickly than large rocks.

questions.question: What is the greatest factor in weathering in the lesson?
choices: Climate
Rock color
Distance from a city
The age of nearby buildings
questions.explanation: Climate is identified as the greatest factor in weathering, with temperature extremes and precipitation emphasized.

questions.question: Which conditions does the lesson emphasize as promoting weathering?
choices: Unchanging temperatures and no precipitation
Little exposure and no water
Only darkness and low air pressure
Extreme temperatures and lots of precipitation
questions.explanation: The climate section emphasizes extreme temperatures and lots of precipitation.

questions.question: What is topography?
choices: The speed of a glacier
The oxygen content of a rock
The surface features of a region
The chemical composition of rain
questions.explanation: Topography describes a region's surface features.

questions.question: Why can mountaintops experience strong weathering and loss of particles?
choices: They collect all the water flowing out of valleys
They are protected from temperature changes
They have greater temperature extremes, and gravity pulls particles away
They never experience freezing or thawing
questions.explanation: The lesson links mountaintops with temperature extremes and particles being pulled away by gravity.

questions.question: Why can valleys have more biological weathering?
choices: They experience no chemical reactions
They collect water
They contain no living things
They prevent roots from growing
questions.explanation: The lesson says valleys collect water and have more biological weathering.

questions.question: What is erosion?
choices: The removal and transport of material by wind, water, ice, or gravity
The breakdown of rock without any movement
A chemical change that creates rust
The expansion of water as it freezes
questions.explanation: Erosion removes material and transports it by wind, water, ice, or gravity.

questions.question: Which example shows erosion following weathering?
choices: A rock cracks but every piece stays in place
Iron combines with oxygen and stays in place
A root widens a crack without moving the fragments away
A rock breaks into pieces, and water carries the pieces away
questions.explanation: Breaking the rock is weathering; carrying the pieces away is erosion.

questions.question: What is mass wasting?
choices: Rock breakdown caused only by oxygen
The formation of sand dunes by wind
The movement of water vapor into the atmosphere
Downhill movement of loose rocks and soil due to gravity
questions.explanation: Gravity causes loose rock and soil to move downhill in mass wasting.

questions.question: What is regolith?
choices: A large mass of moving ice
A chemical compound formed by oxidation
The loose layer of rock and soil
The solid bedrock beneath all loose material
questions.explanation: Regolith is the loose layer of rock and soil above bedrock.

questions.question: What is a mudflow?
choices: Rock breakdown by a chemical reaction with water
Rapid downhill movement of a large mass of mud
Extremely slow downhill movement of dry soil
A long tear-shaped mound of till
questions.explanation: A mudflow is a large mass of mud moving rapidly downhill.

questions.question: Which form of mass wasting is classified as fastest?
choices: Mudflow
Landslide
Earthflow
Soil creep
questions.explanation: The lesson classifies mudflow as the fastest form of mass wasting.

questions.question: What is a landslide in this lesson?
choices: Rapid downhill movement of a large amount of rock and soil
Sediment deposited in sorted layers by a glacier
Extremely slow movement of soil
A depression scooped out by wind
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a landslide as rapid downhill movement of a large amount of rock and soil.

questions.question: What is an earthflow in this lesson?
choices: Rapid movement of a large mass of mud
Sediment carried by a glacier to another region
A chemical reaction involving carbonic acid
Slow movement of soil down a steep slope
questions.explanation: Earthflow is described as slow movement of soil down a steep slope.

questions.question: Which process is described as the slowest form of mass wasting?
choices: Landslide
Mudflow
Soil creep
Earthflow
questions.explanation: Soil creep is an extremely slow downhill slide of soil and is classified as the slowest form of mass wasting.

questions.question: Fence posts on a slope gradually tilt as soil inches downhill. What process does this illustrate?
choices: Ice wedging
Soil creep
Mudflow
Oxidation
questions.explanation: The soil-creep illustration shows leaning fence posts associated with extremely slow downhill soil movement.

questions.question: How does the lesson define slump?
choices: A rock carried between regions by a glacier
An extremely slow downhill slide of soil
A rapid downhill movement of mud
A long tear-shaped mound of till
questions.explanation: Slump is defined in the lesson as an extremely slow downhill slide of soil.

questions.question: Which sequence puts the four listed forms of mass wasting from fastest to slowest?
choices: Mudflow, landslide, earthflow, soil creep
Soil creep, earthflow, landslide, mudflow
Landslide, earthflow, soil creep, mudflow
Earthflow, mudflow, soil creep, landslide
questions.explanation: The lesson labels mudflow fastest, landslide fast, earthflow slow, and soil creep slowest.

questions.question: What is abrasion?
choices: The chemical reaction of a substance with oxygen
The buildup of ice in a glacier
The slow movement of soil down a slope
The wearing away of surfaces by small particles
questions.explanation: The wind erosion notes define abrasion as the wearing away of surfaces by small particles.

questions.question: Windblown particles repeatedly strike a rock and wear its surface away. Which process is this?
choices: Carbonation
Soil creep
Abrasion
Hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Small particles wearing away a surface is abrasion.

questions.question: What is a rock pedestal?
choices: A large mass of moving ice
A loose layer of rock and soil
A mushroom-shaped rock formed by wind
A long tear-shaped mound of glacial till
questions.explanation: The notes describe a rock pedestal as a mushroom-shaped rock formed by wind.

questions.question: What feature is a soil depression formed by the scooping action of wind?
choices: A glacier
A deflation hollow
A drumlin
A rock pedestal
questions.explanation: The wind erosion notes label the wind-scooped soil depression a deflation hollow.

questions.question: What is a dune in the wind erosion notes?
choices: A mound of sand deposited by wind
A boulder transported by a glacier
A chemically weathered piece of limestone
A rapid flow of rock and soil downhill
questions.explanation: The notes describe a dune as a mound of sand deposited by wind on the leeward side of a barrier.

questions.question: On which side of a barrier do the notes show wind depositing sand to build a dune?
choices: The windward side
Equally on every side
Only directly beneath the barrier
The leeward side
questions.explanation: The dune annotation specifies deposition on the leeward side of a barrier.

questions.question: What is a glacier?
choices: Any small patch of frozen water
A mound of windblown sand
A rapid downhill movement of mud
A large mass of moving ice
questions.explanation: A glacier is defined as a large mass of moving ice.

questions.question: What causes a glacier to move in the lesson's explanation?
choices: Carbonic acid dissolves its upper surface into moving soil
Oxidation turns the lower ice into loose rock
Tons of ice compress it, melting the lower layers so it flows slowly along
Wind lifts the entire glacier and carries it downhill
questions.explanation: The lesson explains glacier movement through compression by tons of ice, melting lower layers, and slow grinding flow.

questions.question: What average glacier movement does the lesson give?
choices: 10 inches per year
10 inches per day
10 feet per hour
10 miles per day
questions.explanation: The glacier slide gives an average movement of 10 inches per day.

questions.question: What is glacial drift?
choices: Sediments deposited by glaciers as they advance or retreat
Only the ice that breaks off a glacier
Sand deposited by wind behind a barrier
Rock that breaks down through oxidation
questions.explanation: Glacial drift consists of sediment deposited by glaciers during advance or retreat.

questions.question: What is till?
choices: Unsorted rocks and sediments deposited by a glacier
Sediment sorted by weight before deposition
A large mass of moving ice
A mushroom-shaped rock made by wind
questions.explanation: Till is unsorted rock and sediment deposited by a glacier.

questions.question: What is layered drift in the lesson?
choices: Unsorted rock and sediment deposited directly by a glacier
A large boulder carried from one region to another
A loose layer of rock and soil on a hillside
Material sorted by weight before being deposited
questions.explanation: The lesson describes layered drift as material sorted by weight before deposition.

questions.question: What distinguishes till from layered drift?
choices: Till is ice; layered drift is mud
Till is deposited by wind; layered drift is deposited by gravity alone
Till is unsorted; layered drift is sorted before deposition
Till is sorted; layered drift is unsorted
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts unsorted till with drift sorted by weight before deposition.

questions.question: What is a drumlin?
choices: A layer of rock chemically changed by acid rain
A long tear-shaped mound of till
A mushroom-shaped rock made by wind
A depression scooped out by wind
questions.explanation: A drumlin is a long tear-shaped mound of till.

questions.question: How does the lesson describe a drumlin forming?
choices: Carbonic acid reacts with a limestone surface
A glacier pauses to deposit till and then advances
Wind piles sand behind a barrier
Water freezes and expands inside a crack
questions.explanation: The drumlin slide describes a glacier pausing to deposit till and then advancing.

questions.question: What are glacial erratics?
choices: Enormous boulders carried by glaciers from one area to another
Small sand grains carried only by wind
Soil moving extremely slowly down a slope
Rock compounds broken down by reaction with water
questions.explanation: The lesson describes erratics as enormous boulders transported between areas by glaciers.

questions.question: A long tear-shaped hill consists of unsorted sediment left by a glacier. Which pairing identifies the hill and its material?
choices: Dune and layered drift
Rock pedestal and regolith
Deflation hollow and rust
Drumlin and till
questions.explanation: A drumlin is a long tear-shaped mound of till, and till is unsorted glacial sediment.

questions.question: What is a moraine in the glacier notes?
choices: A long tear-shaped mound of till
A long horizontal formation made as a glacier pushes material
A mushroom-shaped rock formed by wind
A soil depression formed by wind
questions.explanation: The notes describe a moraine as a long horizontal formation caused by a glacier pushing material.

questions.question: Which landform can result when a glacier carves a path through mountains?
choices: A rock pedestal
A sand dune
A deflation hollow
A glacial valley
questions.explanation: The glacier illustration shows a valley left along the glacier's path through mountains.

questions.question: A large body of ice remains in one place without moving. Which feature from the notes would it need to qualify as a glacier?
choices: Movement of the ice
A covering of loose soil
Layers of sorted sediment
A single enormous boulder
questions.explanation: The definition requires a large mass of moving ice; size and ice alone do not satisfy it.

questions.question: Two glacial deposits are examined. Deposit A mixes large rocks with small particles; Deposit B separates particles into layers. How should they be classified?
choices: Both are layered drift because both were deposited
A is till; B is layered drift
A is layered drift; B is till
Both are till because both contain rock
questions.explanation: The till sketch mixes particles, while the layered-drift sketch groups them into layers.

questions.question: What do till and layered drift have in common despite their different arrangements?
choices: Both must be single enormous boulders
Both must be long tear-shaped hills
Both belong to the sediments left by glaciers
Both must form mushroom-shaped rocks
questions.explanation: Glacial drift is sediment deposited by glaciers; till and layered drift are two forms described in the notes.

questions.question: A glacier cuts into a mountain valley, carries pieces of rock away, and leaves them farther along its path. Which part of this sequence is erosion?
choices: Leaving the carried pieces behind
Sorting the carried pieces before leaving them
Freezing meltwater without moving rock
Removing and transporting the rock pieces
questions.explanation: Erosion is the removal and transport of material, so carrying rock away from the valley is the erosion step.

questions.question: An enormous boulder was carried by a glacier from one region to another. How could finding its original region help study that glacier?
choices: It could connect the boulder's source with a place the glacier carried it
It could reveal the exact date the glacier melted
It could show the glacier's exact daily speed
It could show that every glacier traveled the same route
questions.explanation: An erratic was transported between areas, so identifying its source can help connect locations along the glacier's travel.

questions.question: A glacier leaves one enormous boulder at Site A and a long tear-shaped hill of till at Site B. Which labels fit the two sites?
choices: A is a moraine; B is layered drift
A is an erratic; B is a drumlin
A is a drumlin; B is an erratic
A is layered drift; B is an erratic
questions.explanation: An erratic is a transported boulder; a drumlin is a tear-shaped mound of till.

questions.question: Which observation best separates a moraine from a drumlin using the descriptions in the notes?
choices: A moraine is a single boulder; a drumlin is a mushroom-shaped rock
A moraine forms by wind; a drumlin forms by acid rain
A moraine forms a long horizontal feature; a drumlin is a tear-shaped mound
A moraine is moving ice; a drumlin is frozen water that never moves
questions.explanation: The notes describe moraine as a long horizontal formation and drumlin as a long tear-shaped mound of till.

questions.question: A student says sediment left while a glacier retreats cannot be glacial drift. Which correction follows the notes?
choices: Glacial drift is left only during advance
Glacial drift is left only when ice stops moving permanently
Glacial drift is another name for the moving ice itself
Glacial drift can be left during either advance or retreat
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly include sediment deposited as glaciers advance or retreat.

questions.question: A glacier has disappeared from an area. Which finding would still provide evidence that it once carried rock there?
choices: An erratic traced to a different source region
Rust forming on a locally made iron nail
A dune currently growing behind a wind barrier
Roots widening a crack in local stone
questions.explanation: A transported erratic remains evidence of rock carried from elsewhere even after the glacier is gone.

questions.question: How do the glacier's actions differ when making a valley and when making a moraine in the notes?
choices: It leaves both as single transported boulders
It removes material from the valley and pushes material into a formation at the moraine
It builds both by piling windblown sand
It forms both by reacting rock with carbonic acid
questions.explanation: The valley sketch shows a glacier-cut path; the moraine definition describes pushed material forming a long horizontal feature.
